request.user:
Change c0105. Location: 1818 Vol. I, Ch. IV; 1831 Ch. V.

Context before (unchanged): Clerval continued talking for some time about our mutual friends, and his own good fortune in being permitted to come to Ingolstadt.

1818 text: "You may easily believe," said he, "how great was the difficulty to persuade my father that it was not absolutely necessary for a merchant not to understand any thing except book-keeping; and, indeed, I believe I left him incredulous to the last, for his constant answer to my unwearied entreaties was the same as that of the Dutch schoolmaster in the Vicar of Wakefield: 'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek.'

1831 text: "You may easily believe," said he, "how great was the difficulty to persuade my father that all necessary knowledge was not comprised in the noble art of book-keeping; and, indeed, I believe I left him incredulous to the last, for his constant answer to my unwearied entreaties was the same as that of the Dutch schoolmaster in the Vicar of Wakefield:—'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek.'

Diff: " You may easily believe, " said he, " how great was the difficulty to persuade my father that [-it was not absolutely-] {+all+} necessary [-for a merchant-] {+knowledge was+} not [-to understand any thing except-] {+comprised in the noble art of+} book-keeping; and, indeed, I believe I left him incredulous to the last, for his constant answer to my unwearied entreaties was the same as that of the Dutch schoolmaster in the Vicar of Wakefield: {+—+} 'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek. '

Context after (unchanged): But his affection for me at length overcame his dislike of learning, and he has permitted me to undertake a voyage of discovery to the land of knowledge."

result.rationale: The father's view is recast from 'not necessary for a merchant not to understand any thing except book-keeping' to 'all necessary knowledge was not comprised in the noble art of book-keeping'. The meaning is kept, but the scope widens from merchants to knowledge in general, and 'noble art' adds mild irony.
